title: Snakes, eagles, and so-called sorcery
source_text: Ἑξῆς δὲ τούτοις ὡσπερεὶ ἐπὶ πλεῖον καταβιβάσαι ἀγωνιζόμενος τὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένος καὶ ἐξομοιῶσαι τοῖς ἀλόγοις καὶ μηδὲν ὅ τι καταλιπεῖν θέλων τῶν ἐν τοῖς ἀλόγοις ἱστορουμένων ἐμφαινόντων τὸ μεῖζον, καὶ τὰ τῆς γοητείας φησὶν εἶναι καὶ ἔν τισι τῶν ἀλόγων· ὡς μηδ᾿ ἐπὶ τούτῳ τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἐξαιρέτως σεμνύνεσθαι μηδὲ θέλειν ἔχειν τὴν πρὸς τὰ ἄλογα ὑπεροχήν· καί φησι ταῦτα· εἰ δέ τι καὶ (ἐπὶ) γοητείᾳ φρονοῦσιν ἄνθρωποι, ἤδη καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο σοφώτεροι ὄφεις καὶ ἀετοί· πολλὰ γοῦν ἴσασιν ἀλεξιφάρμακα καὶ ἀλεξίκακα καὶ δὴ καὶ λίθων τινῶν δυνάμεις ἐπὶ σωτηρίᾳ τῶν νεοσσῶν. οἷς ἂν ἐπιτύχωσιν ἄνθρωποι, θαυμαστόν τι κτῆμα ἔχειν νομίζουσι. καὶ πρῶτόν γε οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅπως τὴν τῶν ζῴων περὶ τὰ φυσικὰ ἀλεξιφάρμακα εἴτε ἐμπειρίαν εἴτε φυσικήν τινα κατάληψιν γοητείαν ὠνόμασεν· ἐπ᾿ ἄλλου γὰρ τέτριπται τὸ τῆς γοητείας τάσσεσθαι ὄνομα· εἰ μὴ ἄρα λεληθότως διαβάλλειν βούλεται ὡς Ἐπικούρειος πᾶσαν τὴν τῶν τοιούτων χρῆσιν ὡς ἐν ἐπαγγελίᾳ γοήτων κειμένην. πλὴν ἀλλὰ δεδόσθω αὐτῷ τὸ τοὺς ἀνθρώπους φρονεῖν ἐπὶ τῇ τούτων γνώσει μέγα, εἴτε γόητας ὄντας εἴτε καὶ μή· πῶς ὅτι σοφώτεροι κατὰ τοῦτο ἀνθρώπων εἰσὶν ὄφεις τῷ μαράθῳ εἰς ὀξυωπίαν καὶ ταχυτῆτα κινήσεως χρώμενοι. μόνον τοῦτο φυσικὸν οὐκ ἐξ ἐπιλογισμοῦ καταλαμβάνοντες ἀλλ᾿ ἐκ κατασκευῆς; ἄνθρωποι δὲ οὐκ ἀπὸ ψιλῆς φύσεως ἐπὶ τὸ τοιοῦτον ὁμοίως ὄφεσιν ἔρχονται· ἀλλὰ πῇ μὲν ἐκ πείρας πῇ δ᾿ ἐκ λόγου. ἔσθ᾿ ὅτε δ᾿ ἐξ ἐπιλογισμοῦ καὶ κατ᾿ ἐπιστήμην. ὡς εἰ καὶ ἀετοὶ πρὸς σωτηρίαν τῶν ἐν τῇ καλιᾷ νεοσσῶν τὸν λεγόμενον ἀετίτην λίθον εὑρόντες φέρουσιν ἐπ᾿ αὐτὴν, πόθεν ὅτι σοφοὶ ἀετοὶ καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων σοφώτεροι, τῶν ἐκ πείρας τὸ τοῖς ἀετοῖς δοθὲν φυσικὸν βοήθημα εὑρόντων διὰ τὸν λογισμὸν καὶ μετὰ νοῦ χρησαμένων;
pass_a_gloss: Next after these [things], as if striving (ἀγωνιζόμενος) to bring down (καταβιβάσαι) further the race of men and to liken (ἐξομοιῶσαι) [it] to the irrational (ἄλογα), and wishing to leave out nothing of the things recorded (ἱστορουμένων) among the irrational that show (ἐμφαινόντων) the greater, he says the [things] of sorcery (γοητεία) are also in some of the irrational; so that not even on this should men pride themselves (σεμνύνεσθαι) specially (ἐξαιρέτως), nor wish to have superiority (ὑπεροχή) over the irrational. And he says: CELSUS: 'If men think highly (φρονοῦσιν) also on sorcery, already in this too snakes and eagles [are] wiser. At any rate they know many antidotes (ἀλεξιφάρμακα) and averters of harm (ἀλεξίκακα) and also powers (δυνάμεις) of certain stones for the safety (σωτηρία) of the nestlings (νεοσσοί); which if men happen upon, they think they have some marvellous possession (κτῆμα).' ORIGEN: And first, I do not know how he named sorcery the animals' experience (ἐμπειρία) or some natural apprehension (φυσικὴ κατάληψις) about natural antidotes; for the name of sorcery is worn [by usage] (τέτριπται) to be applied to another thing; unless perhaps he wishes covertly (λεληθότως) to slander (διαβάλλειν), as an Epicurean, all use (χρῆσις) of such things as lying in the profession (ἐπαγγελία) of sorcerers (γόητες). But let it be granted him that men think greatly of the knowledge of these, whether being sorcerers or not; how [is it] that in this snakes are wiser than men, using fennel (μάραθον) for sharpness of sight (ὀξυωπία) and swiftness of movement, grasping only this natural thing not from reasoning (ἐπιλογισμός) but from constitution (κατασκευή)? Men do not come to such a thing from bare nature (ψιλὴ φύσις) like snakes, but partly from trial (πεῖρα), partly from reason (λόγος), and sometimes from reasoning-out (ἐπιλογισμός) and according to knowledge (ἐπιστήμη). So, even if eagles, for safety of the nestlings in the nest (καλιά), finding the so-called eagle-stone (ἀετίτης λίθος), carry [it] to it, whence [follows it] that eagles are wise and wiser than men, [men] having found from trial the natural aid (βοήθημα) given to eagles through reasoning (λογισμός) and having used [it] with mind (νοῦς)?
pass_b_english: Next, as though he were straining to drag the human race still lower and make it like the irrational animals, and wished to leave out nothing recorded of the irrational animals that points to something greater in them, he says that the arts of sorcery are found in some of the irrational animals too, so that men should not pride themselves on this either, as something peculiar to them, nor wish to hold superiority over the irrational animals. He says this: “If men take any pride in sorcery as well, then in this too snakes and eagles are wiser. At any rate they know many antidotes and remedies against harm, and even the powers of certain stones for the safety of their young. If men happen upon these, they think they possess something marvellous.”

First, I do not know how he came to give the name sorcery to the animals’ experience, or some natural grasp, of natural antidotes, for the name sorcery is commonly given to something else; unless, perhaps, as an Epicurean he wishes covertly to discredit all use of such things, as if it belonged to what sorcerers profess. But let it be granted him that men pride themselves greatly on knowing these things, whether they are sorcerers or not. How does it follow that in this respect snakes are wiser than men, because they use fennel to sharpen their sight and quicken their movement? They grasp this single natural thing not by reasoning but from their constitution. Men, however, do not come to such a thing from bare nature, as snakes do, but partly from experience, partly from reason, and sometimes from reflection and by systematic knowledge. So too, even if eagles find the stone called the eagle-stone and carry it to the nest for the safety of the young in it, how does it follow that eagles are wise, and wiser than men, when men found by experience the natural aid given to eagles and, through reasoning, used it with understanding?

choices.choice: Folded 'His aim is that men should not...' back into the main sentence as a purpose clause ('so that men should not...'), matching ὡς μηδ᾿ ... σεμνύνεσθαι and removing the added 'His aim is'
Celsus: 'If men pride themselves on sorcery as well' to 'If men take any pride in sorcery as well' (keeps τι in εἰ δέ τι ... φρονοῦσιν)
'how he came to call sorcery the animals’ experience' to 'how he came to give the name sorcery to the animals’ experience' (clearer English order)
Joined the stray 'Unless, perhaps...' fragment to the preceding sentence
Restored 'even' in ὡς εἰ καὶ ἀετοί ('So too, even if eagles...')
Kept the genitive of comparison inside the eagle question ('when men found by experience ... and, through reasoning, used it with understanding') instead of a separate 'For men found...' sentence

Celsus’s words are in double quotation marks; the quotation runs from “If men take any pride” to “something marvellous”. Koetschau supplies (ἐπὶ) before γοητείᾳ; translated as supplied. γοητεία is rendered “sorcery” throughout, keeping Origen’s complaint that Celsus misapplies the word to animal instinct. ἀλεξιφάρμακα καὶ ἀλεξίκακα rendered “antidotes and remedies against harm”. ἐπιλογισμός is rendered “reasoning” in the snake clause and “reflection” in the list of human means, to keep the climb from experience to reason to reflection to systematic knowledge (ἐπιστήμη). The charge that Celsus writes “as an Epicurean” is Origen’s recurring suspicion about him; kept as Origen’s judgement. The closing genitive participles (τῶν … εὑρόντων … χρησαμένων) describe the men of the comparison and are kept inside the question (“when men found …”). The lore of snakes using fennel for their eyes and of eagles placing the aetites (eagle-stone) in the nest is common ancient natural history (compare Pliny, Natural History); no inline source given since neither writer quotes a text. No Scripture in this chapter.
